title: Iran offers to reopen Hormuz in two days if US meets terms, as Trump talks of 'the hammer'
dek: Tehran's foreign ministry called the shorter timetable a sign of good faith after its negotiators left Doha. Trump told an Iowa rally the US may have to give Iran 'the hammer', and Iran claims two more tankers hit its mines.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran said on Monday that it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the United States met its conditions, a day after its negotiators left Doha at the end of three days of talks with Qatari mediators. "The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said, according to Reuters.

The offer came on the eve of Tuesday's US midterm elections and a day after President Donald Trump told a rally in Dubuque, Iowa, that the only reason he had not "finished with Iran" was that he wanted to save lives, but that "at some point we're going to have to give them the hammer", AFP reported. Iran's military answered that any new war would last longer than the last one. Iran's Revolutionary Guards also claimed that two more oil tankers had hit Iranian mines in the strait, a claim that could not be independently verified.

## Monday: Tehran's two-day offer

Baqaei said Tehran had earlier proposed a one-week timetable and was now considering two days. "If Iran's demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period," he said, Reuters reported. He said messages were still being exchanged through mediators.

The Iranian team, led by Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi, left Doha on Sunday. An official briefed on the talks told Reuters the departure was not caused by difficulties in the negotiations. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that consultations on the two-day plan were "moving toward implementation, but we have not yet reached a definitive conclusion", and that meeting an American delegation was "not on the cards", according to IRNA as reported by ANI.

In Washington, the news site Axios reported that Trump was putting diplomacy first despite Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressing, in a Saturday phone call, for strikes soon after the midterms, Anadolu Agency said. Trump called it "a very good talk" and gave no details. At the Manama Dialogue in Bahrain on Sunday, US Assistant Secretary of State Donald Blome said the US was ready for talks but "prepared to go in another direction", adding: "We just can't allow Iran to take this region and the global economy hostage," Al Jazeera reported.

## The latest warnings

Iran's army spokesman, Mohammad Akraminia, said on state television that "a potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion", according to Dawn, citing agencies. A Revolutionary Guards spokesman, Hossein Mohebbi, said that in a conflict with America "there are no geographical limitations".

Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said on Saturday that he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks, and that he had not yet replied, AFP and Dawn reported. Rezaei said Tehran had told Washington that unless its conditions were met, neither would the strait reopen nor would there be negotiations. The White House has not commented on the letter.

Shipping attacks continued. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) reported that a tanker was struck by two projectiles 72 nautical miles east of Ras Al Khafji, on the Saudi-Kuwaiti coast, on Sunday, with all crew accounted for, according to Gulf News. US Central Command rejected the Iranian foreign minister's claim that Tehran had not attacked civilians, saying more than 20 civilian mariners had been killed in recent months, Gulf News reported.

An IRGC Navy spokesperson told the state broadcaster IRIB that both ships were using "an unauthorized route" with their tracking systems switched off, The Jerusalem Post reported. The IRGC gave no ship names, flags or crew figures.

## Background

Iran has now claimed at least six mine strikes on tankers since Friday: four on Friday and Saturday, according to its own statements reported by Gulf News, and the two announced on Sunday night. None has been confirmed by an independent source. Over the same period, the Qatari liquefied natural gas carrier Al Mayeda, with six Indian sailors aboard, was hit by "unidentified objects" in the Gulf, and Oman evacuated 25 crew from a burning Panama-flagged tanker off its Musandam peninsula.

The fighting began on 28 February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran. A ceasefire followed in April, and a US-Iran navigation memorandum was signed in June, but Al Jazeera said it had collapsed by August. Since then the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been the main front.

## What they are saying

Earlier on Sunday Trump said the war would be over "very soon, one way or the other", and that Iran would either agree a deal or "we'll just end it", Al Jazeera reported. On Saturday he said the US still had to "take care of" one or two Iranian sites, including the underground complex known as Pickaxe Mountain, but that he was "not in a hurry". Iran denies carrying out nuclear work there.

Iran's conditions, as set out by Araghchi and reported by Al Jazeera, include lifting recent sanctions, restoring oil waivers granted in June, releasing frozen funds including those held in Qatar, reducing US forces in the region and recognising shipping routes designated by Iran and Oman.

Al Jazeera reported that the US had warned Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense round of fighting after the midterms, and that a senior Israeli official, cited by the Israeli news site Ynet, said Israel was preparing for another round immediately after the vote. Neither government has said so publicly.

## Markets

Oil prices eased on Monday on hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough, with Brent crude down about 1.8% at around $111.4 a barrel in Asian trade, Business Today reported, after it settled at $113.43 on Friday and rose 13.6% over October.

## What it means for India

India buys most of its crude oil abroad, and a large share of its oil and gas imports normally passes through Hormuz, so every reported strike feeds into fuel prices and the import bill. Thousands of Indian sailors also work on ships in the Gulf. The Ministry of External Affairs has said 22 Indian nationals, 14 of them seafarers, have been killed in the West Asia conflict, ANI reported. The government said last week that Indian crew on three ships hit near the strait were all safe; no Indian nationals have been reported aboard the ships named in Sunday's claims.

## What happens next

Americans vote on Tuesday, 3 November. Trump said in October that the US would not attack Iran before the midterms. Whether Washington answers Iran's two-day offer, rejects it, or resumes strikes once the vote is over is now the main question for shipping and for oil importers such as India.

## Key numbers

- Days Iran says it needs to reopen Hormuz once its conditions are met: 2 (down from 7)
- Tanker mine strikes claimed by Iran since Friday: at least six, none independently confirmed
- Projectile attacks recorded by UKMTO in the strait since 6 July: 81
- Indian nationals killed in the West Asia conflict, per the MEA: 22, including 14 seafarers
- Brent crude: about $111.4 on Monday, down about 1.8%
- Civilian mariners killed in recent months, per US Central Command: more than 20
- US midterm elections: Tuesday, 3 November
